glossary: SPF
Sender Policy Framework. A TXT record listing the servers allowed to send mail for a domain. Receivers check it against the envelope sender (Return-Path), not the From: address people see.
DKIM

DomainKeys Identified Mail. The sending service signs each message with a private key; receivers fetch the public key from <selector>._domainkey.<domain> to verify the message was not altered and came from a key the domain owner published.
DMARC

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance. A TXT record at _dmarc.<domain> telling receivers what to do when a message's visible From: domain is not authenticated by an aligned SPF or DKIM pass, and where to send reports.
Alignment
DMARC passes only when the domain authenticated by SPF or DKIM matches (aligns with) the From: domain the recipient sees.
MTA-STS
SMTP MTA Strict Transport Security. Lets a domain require that other mail servers deliver to it only over TLS with a valid certificate, defeating downgrade and interception attacks.
TLS-RPT
SMTP TLS Reporting. A TXT record asking other mail servers to send daily reports about TLS failures when delivering to the domain.
STARTTLS
The SMTP command that upgrades a plaintext mail connection on port 25 to an encrypted TLS connection.
CAA
Certification Authority Authorization. DNS records naming the certificate authorities allowed to issue certificates for the domain.
DNSSEC
DNS Security Extensions. Cryptographic signatures on DNS records, anchored by a DS record at the parent zone, so resolvers can detect forged answers.
DS record
Delegation Signer. Published at the registrar (in the parent zone, such as .org) to link the parent's chain of trust to the domain's DNSSEC keys.
EPP status
Registry status codes such as clientTransferProhibited that control whether a domain can be transferred, updated or deleted.

findings.title: SPF record missing
findings.about: Checks that the domain publishes an SPF record (a TXT record beginning v=spf1) listing the servers allowed to send its mail.
findings.analysis: No SPF record (TXT beginning v=spf1) is published.
findings.what_we_found: No TXT record beginning "v=spf1" is published at test.c4lab.in. Receivers checking SPF for mail from test.c4lab.in get the result "none".
why_it_matters: SPF is how a receiving server asks "is this server allowed to send mail for test.c4lab.in?". With no record, every server on the internet is equally plausible, so receivers cannot use SPF to reject or flag mail sent by an impersonator.
Without SPF, DMARC can pass only through DKIM. Any of your legitimate services that do not sign with DKIM will fail DMARC once you enforce it.
Since February 2024 Google and Yahoo require SPF or DKIM on all mail they accept, and both for bulk senders. Mail from test.c4lab.in is more likely to be sent to spam or rejected.
findings.attack_scenario: An attacker sends mail with the envelope sender and From: address set to someone@test.c4lab.in from their own server. With no SPF (and no enforcing DMARC) the receiving server has no domain policy to apply, so the message is judged only by content filters.
findings.severity_rationale: High when the domain receives mail (it is clearly in active use and worth impersonating); medium when it publishes no MX records. It would be critical only if combined with a missing DMARC record on a domain known to send payment or account mail.
fix_steps: List every service that sends mail as @test.c4lab.in: your mailbox provider (DreamHost Mail), the website and its contact forms, newsletters, CRM, helpdesk and invoicing systems.
Collect the SPF include for each from its documentation.

fix_steps.text: Publish one TXT record at the domain apex. In your DNS hosting provider: Open the control panel of the provider that hosts the domain's DNS (the nameservers listed in this report) and add or edit the record there. A starting point based on the providers detected:

fix_steps: Keep the record to ten or fewer DNS-querying terms (include, a, mx, exists, redirect).
Send a test message to a Gmail address and check "Show original": SPF should show PASS.
findings.rollback: Delete the TXT record; receivers return to SPF "none" within the TTL.

findings.title: DMARC record missing or invalid
findings.about: Checks that exactly one DMARC record (v=DMARC1) is published at _dmarc.<domain>. DMARC tells receivers what to do with mail whose visible From: domain is not authenticated.
findings.analysis: No DMARC record is published at _dmarc.
findings.what_we_found: No TXT record beginning "v=DMARC1" is published at _dmarc.test.c4lab.in.
why_it_matters: SPF and DKIM authenticate technical identities (the envelope sender and the signing domain), not the From: address the recipient reads. DMARC connects the two: it passes only when SPF or DKIM authenticates a domain that aligns with the visible From: domain.
With no DMARC record, receivers have no instruction from you about forged mail and send you no reports, so you cannot see who is sending mail as test.c4lab.in.
Google and Yahoo require a DMARC record for bulk senders (more than 5,000 messages a day to their users), and many receivers treat a missing record as a negative reputation signal.
findings.attack_scenario: An attacker sends mail with From: accounts@test.c4lab.in from their own server, using an envelope domain they control so SPF passes for their domain. The visible From: is yours, there is no DMARC policy to check alignment, and the message reaches the inbox.
findings.severity_rationale: High: exact-domain impersonation is unrestricted and invisible to you. It is not critical because content filtering still applies and no record actively authorises the attacker.

fix_steps.text: Publish a monitoring policy now so reports start arriving. In your DNS hosting provider: Open the control panel of the provider that hosts the domain's DNS (the nameservers listed in this report) and add or edit the record there.

fix_steps: Create the mailbox dmarc-reports@test.c4lab.in (or use a DMARC reporting service) and review the aggregate reports for two to four weeks.
Fix SPF and DKIM for every legitimate sender that the reports show failing.

findings.title: DNSSEC not deployed
findings.about: Checks that the zone is DNSSEC-signed (DNSKEY and RRSIG records) and anchored at the parent zone with a DS record, so resolvers can detect forged DNS answers.
findings.analysis: The zone is not DNSSEC-signed (no DS at the parent, no DNSKEY).
findings.what_we_found: test.c4lab.in is not DNSSEC-signed: the parent zone has no DS record for it and the zone serves no DNSKEY records.
why_it_matters: Without DNSSEC, a resolver cannot tell a genuine answer for test.c4lab.in from a forged one. Cache-poisoning attacks (such as the Kaminsky attack class) or an attacker on the network path can return false A or MX records, sending visitors to a fake website and mail to an attacker's server.
DNSSEC is also the foundation for DANE, which lets mail servers pin your MX certificates in DNS.
findings.attack_scenario: A poisoned resolver at an ISP or on public Wi-Fi returns the attacker's IP address for test.c4lab.in. Visitors reach a cloned site (HTTPS warnings are the remaining defence), and other mail servers deliver mail for test.c4lab.in to the attacker's MX.
findings.severity_rationale: Medium: forged DNS requires a privileged position or a resolver weakness, and HTTPS still protects web users who heed warnings. Most domains remain unsigned, but DNSSEC removes a whole class of redirection attacks.
fix_steps: Enable signing at the DNS host. your DNS hosting provider: Enable DNSSEC signing at the DNS hosting provider, then add the DS record it gives you at the registrar.
Copy the DS record values (key tag, algorithm, digest type and digest) that the DNS host gives you.
Add the DS record at the registrar. GoDaddy: In GoDaddy open Domain Portfolio → the domain → DNS → DNSSEC → Add DS record.
Wait for the parent zone to publish the DS record (usually under an hour; up to 48 hours for some TLDs), then verify.
Important: if you ever move DNS hosting, remove the DS record at the registrar first and wait for its TTL to expire before switching, or validating resolvers will treat the domain as broken.
findings.rollback: Remove the DS record at the registrar first, wait for the parent TTL, then turn off signing.

why_it_matters: If that server is unreachable, every service on the domain (website, email, APIs) stops resolving once caches expire.

findings.title: MTA-STS not enforced
findings.about: Checks that the domain publishes an MTA-STS policy in enforce mode, so other mail servers must deliver to it over TLS with a valid certificate.
findings.analysis: No MTA-STS record is published; inbound SMTP TLS can be downgraded.
findings.what_we_found: No MTA-STS record is published at _mta-sts.test.c4lab.in, so other mail servers have no instruction to require TLS when delivering to test.c4lab.in.
why_it_matters: SMTP between mail servers uses opportunistic TLS. The sending server asks for STARTTLS, but if the request is stripped or the certificate is invalid it normally continues in plaintext rather than failing.

An attacker positioned on the network path (a compromised router, a malicious Wi-Fi network or a BGP/DNS hijack) can remove STARTTLS from the conversation and read or alter mail sent to test.c4lab.in. MTA-STS lets you publish "only deliver to these MX hosts, only over valid TLS", and compliant senders such as Gmail and Microsoft 365 then refuse to downgrade.
findings.attack_scenario: STARTTLS-stripping: an on-path attacker removes the STARTTLS capability from mx1.dreamhost.com's response, and the sender delivers password-reset emails, invoices or contracts to test.c4lab.in in plaintext, readable and modifiable in transit.
findings.severity_rationale: Low: exploitation requires a privileged network position, and major providers already use TLS by default. MTA-STS closes the downgrade gap.

fix_steps.text: Create the policy file. Start in testing mode, listing every MX host:
fix_steps.code:
version: STSv1
mode: testing
mx: mx1.dreamhost.com
max_age: 86400

fix_steps: Serve it at https://mta-sts.test.c4lab.in/.well-known/mta-sts.txt with a valid certificate for mta-sts.test.c4lab.in. Any static web host works: add the subdomain at your web host, or use a service such as Cloudflare Workers, GitHub Pages or your email provider's hosted MTA-STS.

fix_steps.text: Announce it in DNS. Change the id whenever the policy changes. In your DNS hosting provider: Open the control panel of the provider that hosts the domain's DNS (the nameservers listed in this report) and add or edit the record there.

fix_steps: Publish TLS-RPT (see S18-TLSRPT-001) so you receive failure reports.
After two to four weeks of clean TLS reports, change mode to enforce, raise max_age to 604800 (one week) or more, and update the id.
findings.rollback: Set mode: none in the policy file and update the id; remove the record after max_age has passed.

verify.expected: "v=STSv1; id=..." and a policy containing "mode: enforce" with every MX host listed.

Google — About MTA-STS and TLS reporting

findings.title: CAA record missing
findings.about: Checks for CAA records naming the certificate authorities allowed to issue certificates for the domain. Since 2017 every public CA must check CAA before issuing.
findings.analysis: No CAA record; any public CA may issue certificates for the domain.
findings.what_we_found: No CAA records are published for test.c4lab.in, so any of the many publicly trusted certificate authorities may issue certificates for it.
why_it_matters: Certificate authorities validate that a requester controls a domain, but that validation can be fooled: through a hijacked web host or DNS record, a BGP hijack of the validation traffic, or a mistake at one CA. CAA shrinks the attack surface from every public CA to the one or two you actually use.
The certificate currently served on https://test.c4lab.in was issued by your current certificate authority, so a CAA record can name that CA without affecting renewals.
findings.attack_scenario: An attacker who briefly controls a validation path obtains a valid certificate for test.c4lab.in from a CA you do not use, then impersonates the website or intercepts its traffic with no browser warning.
findings.severity_rationale: Low: exploitation requires another weakness to pass CA validation, and Certificate Transparency logs would record the rogue certificate. CAA is a cheap hardening step.

fix_steps.text: Publish CAA records naming your CA (<your CA's CAA domain, for example letsencrypt.org>) and an incident contact. In your DNS hosting provider: Open the control panel of the provider that hosts the domain's DNS (the nameservers listed in this report) and add or edit the record there.
fix_steps.code:
test.c4lab.in.  3600  IN  CAA  0 issue "<your CA's CAA domain, for example letsencrypt.org>"
test.c4lab.in.  3600  IN  CAA  0 issuewild ";"
test.c4lab.in.  3600  IN  CAA  0 iodef "mailto:security@test.c4lab.in"

fix_steps: Add an issue line for every other CA that issues for the domain or its subdomains (for example a CDN, mail provider or managed hosting platform). Check existing certificates at https://crt.sh/?q=test.c4lab.in before publishing.
issuewild ";" forbids wildcard certificates; omit that line if you use wildcards.
findings.rollback: Delete the CAA records; issuance is unrestricted again immediately after the TTL.

verify.expected: 0 issue "<your CA's CAA domain, for example letsencrypt.org>" (plus any others you added).

findings.remediation: Publish CAA records naming your CA (<your CA's CAA domain, for example letsencrypt.org>) and an incident contact. In your DNS hosting provider: Open the control panel of the provider that hosts the domain's DNS (the nameservers listed in this report) and add or edit the record there.

findings.title: SMTP TLS reporting not configured
findings.about: Checks that the domain publishes a TLS-RPT record (_smtp._tls) so other mail servers report TLS delivery failures to the owner.
findings.analysis: No TLS-RPT record; SMTP TLS delivery failures are not reported to the owner.
findings.what_we_found: No TXT record beginning "v=TLSRPTv1" is published at _smtp._tls.test.c4lab.in.
why_it_matters: Without TLS-RPT you are not told when other servers fail to establish TLS with your MX hosts, whether from an expired certificate, a misconfiguration or an active downgrade attack. It is also the feedback loop needed before switching MTA-STS to enforce.
findings.attack_scenario: Interception attempts and certificate problems on inbound mail go unnoticed.
findings.severity_rationale: Informational: reporting only, with no direct protection.
